input:
The picture that emerges from the reported lifetimes is, on closer inspection, a somewhat confusing one, because the two groups that have studied the benchmark material report lifetime values that differ from one another by a margin that is too large to be explained away as ordinary scatter. Both groups were working with materials of the same class, and both describe careful measurement programmes, so the discrepancy cannot simply be attributed to carelessness on one side or the other, and it deserves to be examined in terms of the conditions under which the measurements were actually made.

The conditions, it turns out, were far from identical. In one programme, the material was exposed continuously to a feed that carried moisture, and its lifetime was recorded as the time over which its performance declined under that exposure. In the other programme, the feed was dry, and the material was taken through repeated cycles of use and regeneration, so that the reported lifetime reflects survival under cycling rather than under continuous exposure to a challenging feed. These are, in effect, measurements of two different kinds of endurance, and it is perhaps not surprising that they lead to different numbers.

On balance, and with some hesitation, the values obtained under the moist feed appear to be the more relevant guide for the benchmark material where the intended service involves a feed that carries moisture, since those values were earned under conditions that resemble that service more closely. The preference is, however, a limited and a conditional one, and it rests on that resemblance.
target:
Lifetime is the quantity on which the two groups disagree most sharply. Both report on the same class of material, and both report on the benchmark material directly, yet the lifetime values stand far enough apart that neither can be absorbed into the scatter of the other. The disagreement survives the obvious explanations: the measurement programmes are both described in detail, and neither group reports conditions that would make its own value an outlier on its own terms.

The test conditions differ in the feed and in the duty cycle, and the difference is enough to account for the gap. One group held the material under continuous exposure to a feed carrying moisture, and lifetime in that programme is endurance against a wet feed. The other group worked with a dry feed and took the material through repeated cycles of use and regeneration, so lifetime there is endurance against cycling. The two programmes measure different failure routes, and a value from one cannot be used to correct a value from the other.

A limited preference follows. Where the intended service carries moisture in the feed, the values from the moist-feed programme are the better guide for the benchmark material, because they were earned against the failure route that service imposes. The preference rests on that condition and reaches no further: for dry, cycling duty the other programme is the relevant one, and neither set of values displaces it there.
